classification.difficultyReason: Explain reversed orientation and construct transformations in prescribed orders, choosing suitable rotation centres and diagonal reflection lines so both orientation and position match.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 extends the rectangle transformations in Example 1 to scalene triangles with reversed orientation. The directly assessed skill is recognising congruence through rigid motions.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of rigid motions and Example 1’s ordered grid transformations, specifying rotation centres, reflection lines and translation distances.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires explaining reversed orientation and describing four ordered combinations of rigid motions.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding vertices and combine marked givens with shared sides, vertically opposite angles or alternate angles.

questions.mappingNote: All ten figures directly assess selecting a congruent-triangle test; naming corresponding vertices is a supporting skill. Parts a and j use SSS; b and e use SAS; c uses ASA; d uses alternate angles and shared BD with ASA; f and h use RHS; g and i use AAS.
questions.methodNote: Use SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS or RHS, explicitly identify the three corresponding givens and preserve vertex order. Page 4 treats ASA and AAS as equivalent; page 5 demonstrates shared sides, vertically opposite angles and right triangles. Page 6 excludes SSA.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding vertices and combine marked givens with shared sides, vertically opposite angles or alternate angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires proving both directions using triangle congruence.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is a two-direction proof of an equilateral-triangle property.
questions.methodNote: Use the congruence criteria and corresponding-side/angle conclusions; page 6 proves both directions of the isosceles-triangle result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires proving both directions using triangle congruence.

classification.difficultyReason: Select congruence criteria and use corresponding parts to prove midpoint and parallel-line conclusions.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess constructing congruence proofs and drawing corresponding-part conclusions.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 treats ASA and AAS as equivalent tests. Page 5 demonstrates SAS using vertically opposite angles and formal corresponding-vertex statements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select congruence criteria and use corresponding parts to prove midpoint and parallel-line conclusions.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied subquestions guide an SSS proof using the midpoint and shared side, then link corresponding angles to equal supplementary angles and perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: The practical frame supplies an isosceles triangle; the scaffold directly assesses congruence and its angle consequences.
questions.methodNote: Use the SSS proof structure demonstrated on page 5 and the corresponding-angle consequence illustrated on page 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: A scaffolded practical proof uses SSS, corresponding angles and supplementary angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the congruent-triangle hint to select the two triangles, extract equal sides from the construction radii, and translate corresponding equal angles into the bisector conclusion.

questions.mappingNote: The construction supplies equal radii and a shared side; the assessed conclusion follows from congruent triangles.
questions.methodNote: Establish three corresponding equal sides, apply SSS congruence, then deduce equality of corresponding angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify equal radii and a shared side, establish SSS congruence, and deduce that a ray bisects an angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Build a linked congruence argument from the circle radii: establish angle bisection first, then use smaller congruent triangles to prove both equal segments and perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is constructing a congruence proof establishing perpendicularity and equal segment lengths.
questions.methodNote: Use SSS and SAS congruence, equal radii and corresponding parts, followed by the angle sum on a straight line. The worked proof makes explicit the congruence needed to justify the teacher answer's 30-degree angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a sequence of congruence arguments to prove both midpoint and perpendicular properties of a compass construction.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer equal sides from compass constructions, prove SSS congruence and use corresponding alternate angles to establish parallel lines.

questions.mappingNote: This construction requires SSS congruence using equal radii and a shared side, then the converse of the alternate-angle property; constructing proofs using congruent triangles is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: The teaching establishes SSS and formal side-equality proofs, followed by deductions from corresponding angles of congruent triangles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer equal sides from compass constructions, prove SSS congruence and use corresponding alternate angles to establish parallel lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Count corresponding square sides on a grid and divide image length by original length.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly assesses the Example 1 method for square images, including one reduction and one enlargement.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 divides an image side length by the corresponding original side length, counting grid intervals. Examples 2 and 3 distinguish enlargement about a centre from determining a linear scale factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count corresponding square sides on a grid and divide image length by original length.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each vertex's displacement from the supplied centre, double it, and join the image vertices using the taught enlargement procedure.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies that construction with scale factor 2 to a triangle on a square grid.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 places image vertices on rays from O with image distances equal to the scale factor times the original distances.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a factor-2 enlargement on a supplied square grid about a marked centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply the square vertices' displacements from the given centre by three and connect the resulting points; no method selection is required.

questions.mappingNote: The same enlargement method is directly assessed with a square rather than a triangle.
questions.methodNote: Use the centre-based factor-3 construction demonstrated in Example 2, scaling each vertex’s displacement from O.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a factor-3 enlargement of a unit square about a marked centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied half-scale factor to each displacement from the centre, placing image vertices halfway towards the original vertices.

questions.mappingNote: This is the reduction case of the taught centre-based scaling method.
questions.methodNote: Apply OA′=k×OA from page 9 with k=1/2, using Example 2’s vertex-by-vertex construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a reduction by placing vertices halfway from a marked centre to the original square.

classification.difficultyReason: Locate each image vertex halfway from the given centre to its original vertex and join them, directly applying the taught reduction construction.

questions.mappingNote: The response directly assesses applying a scale factor to construct a reduced figure.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 scales distances from O along rays through corresponding vertices. Apply the same construction with scale factor one half.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a reduction on a grid about a specified centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Match corresponding vertices to intersect their joining lines, compare grid lengths for the scale factor, and square that factor for area; each method is explicitly taught and separately prompted.

questions.mappingNote: Part (c) assesses area ratios of similar figures, the most advanced directly assessed skill; parts (a) and (b) support it through linear scaling and graphical construction.
questions.methodNote: Divide corresponding side lengths for the linear scale factor. Example 3 finds the centre by intersecting lines through corresponding vertices, and its continuation states that area scales by k squared.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine a linear scale factor and graphical centre, then square the factor to relate areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Match corners of nested squares and extend their joining lines to locate an interior centre, then use the side ratio and its square for the requested factors.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 directly applies Example 3 and its continuation on page 11 to nested squares.
questions.methodNote: Divide corresponding side lengths; intersect lines through corresponding vertices to find the centre; square the length scale factor for area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine an enlargement centre between grid intersections and relate length and area scale factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify matching triangle vertices, find the centre from intersecting corresponding-vertex lines, and apply the taught length-ratio and squared-area rules.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 extends the graphical centre construction of Examples 2–3 and the general area rule on page 11 to triangles.
questions.methodNote: Compare corresponding lengths, intersect corresponding-vertex lines and use the area multiplier k squared.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use corresponding triangle sides, graphical construction and the squared area scale factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify similarity using shared and parallel-line angles, express the whole side as x+2, and solve the resulting corresponding-side proportion with x on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: This item directly assesses a similarity proof followed by a length calculation.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 Example 1 establishes AAA similarity using shared and corresponding angles, then equates whole-base and corresponding-side ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish similarity using parallel-line angles, then solve a corresponding-side proportion involving a whole base.

classification.difficultyReason: Match vertices across the hourglass using vertically opposite and alternate angles, then set up and solve a direct corresponding-side proportion.

questions.mappingNote: The hourglass orientation changes the angle reasons but preserves the taught AAA-and-ratio method.
questions.methodNote: Apply the page 13 AAA test using vertically opposite and parallel-line angles, then equate corresponding-side ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select AAA or SAS from the diagram's givens, preserve vertex correspondence and solve a side proportion.

classification.difficultyReason: Select SAS similarity from two proportional side pairs and the vertically opposite included angle, then use the established correspondence to find the remaining side.

questions.mappingNote: No parallel-line given is printed; the proportional sides and vertically opposite included angle establish SAS.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 states the SAS test; page 15 Example 3 compares two side ratios around an equal included angle before using the remaining corresponding sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select AAA or SAS from the diagram's givens, preserve vertex correspondence and solve a side proportion.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove AAA similarity from the parallel lines, recognise that the corresponding whole base is x+5, and solve the resulting proportion for the extra segment.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed unknown is a segment of the larger triangle, requiring a whole-base expression.
questions.methodNote: Use page 13 Example 1: establish AAA similarity, express the larger base as the sum of its segments, and equate corresponding ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establish similarity using parallel-line angles, then solve a corresponding-side proportion involving a whole base.

classification.difficultyReason: Establish similarity from shared and corresponding angles, then combine proportional corresponding sides with the given equal outer sides to prove the inner sides equal.

questions.mappingNote: The shared angle and corresponding angles from DE parallel to CB establish triangle similarity; the isosceles given then yields equal smaller sides.
questions.methodNote: Use matching vertices, AAA similarity from two equal angle pairs, and equality of corresponding-side ratios, as in page 13 Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses a shared angle and parallel-line angles to establish similarity, then proportional sides to prove equality.

classification.difficultyReason: Track the changed vertex correspondence using the given and shared angles, then assemble both whole sides from segments before forming the proportion for x.

questions.mappingNote: The explicit proof assesses matching vertices A↔D, B↔E, C↔C before solving for the unknown base segment.
questions.methodNote: Use the corresponding-vertex definition on page 12 and the AAA proof followed by corresponding-side ratios in page 13 Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove similarity with the correct vertex correspondence, then use different corresponding sides to find the split base length.

classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the taught equal-area method by relating h to x through similarity, imposing half the total area, and solving the resulting quadratic relation for a positive length.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 changes Example 5's three equal-area regions to two, so the smaller triangle has area 6 rather than 4.
questions.methodNote: AAA similarity gives the smaller height in terms of its base; Example 5 then substitutes this into the required fraction of the total triangle area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine triangle similarity with equal areas to obtain an exact surd length.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding sides in a differently oriented right triangle and combine similarity with equal areas.

questions.mappingNote: The perpendicular-to-hypotenuse divider changes the orientation of the smaller triangle. Its leg x corresponds to the whole triangle's leg 3, while its other perpendicular leg corresponds to 4.
questions.methodNote: Identify similar triangles using equal angles, pair corresponding sides, and substitute their relationship into the smaller triangle's required area, following Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify corresponding sides in a differently oriented right triangle and combine similarity with equal areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Identifies similar right triangles in a mirror situation and pairs their corresponding heights and ground distances.

questions.mappingNote: Page 13 teaches AAA similarity followed by a corresponding-side ratio to determine an unknown length; this question applies that sequence to the mirror model.
questions.methodNote: Identify similar right triangles using equal angles, then equate corresponding-side ratios.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies similar right triangles in a mirror situation and pairs their corresponding heights and ground distances.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify two pairs of similar triangles and combine their corresponding-side ratios to determine the crossing height.

questions.mappingNote: The practical crossing-cable configuration requires matching perpendicular heights and horizontal distances in similar triangles.
questions.methodNote: Establish AAA similarity and equate ratios of corresponding sides, retaining exact arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify two pairs of similar triangles and combine their corresponding-side ratios to determine the crossing height.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the equilateral triangle's height, identify the similar triangle above the square and solve an exact side-ratio equation.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the same inscribed-square method to the equilateral triangle, first deriving its perpendicular height by Pythagoras.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 on pages 15–16 identifies a triangle outside an inscribed square, establishes AAA similarity and solves a corresponding-side ratio involving the square side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the equilateral triangle's height, identify the similar triangle above the square and solve an exact side-ratio equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied reflection construction to connect preserved angles, parallel lines and angle bisection, then convert a similarity ratio involving summed sides into the theorem's segment ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Page 13 teaches angle matching and AAA followed by side ratios. The embedded construction on page 19 supplies the reflection needed for this general proof.
questions.methodNote: Use reflection, corresponding angles, AAA similarity and corresponding-side ratios, followed by exact algebraic rearrangement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses a reflected construction to establish similarity and derive a general side-ratio theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the stated Angle Bisector Theorem to match two side ratios and solve for an unknown segment.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17 directly applies that theorem, pairing the upper opposite-side segment x with side 3 and the lower segment 4 with side 6.
questions.methodNote: Question 16 states the Angle Bisector Theorem: BD/CD = AB/AC.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the stated Angle Bisector Theorem to match two side ratios and solve for an unknown segment.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines two angle-bisector ratios to prove a quadrilateral identity.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the theorem separately at A and C, using the common ratio BE/ED.
questions.methodNote: Question 16 states and proves the Angle Bisector Theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines two angle-bisector ratios to prove a quadrilateral identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Derives the bisector length from a side ratio and a smaller right triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Use the bisector ratio on the hypotenuse and corresponding sides of a smaller right triangle.
questions.methodNote: AAA similarity and the Angle Bisector Theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives the bisector length from a side ratio and a smaller right triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines a directly obtained ratio with a given sum.

questions.mappingNote: BD:CD determines AB:AC; the given sum fixes the common multiplier.
questions.methodNote: Angle Bisector Theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines a directly obtained ratio with a given sum.

classification.difficultyReason: The rotated square requires two similarity ratios and substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) directly adapts Example 4; part (b) requires similarity in the two triangles beside a rotated square.
questions.methodNote: AAA similarity and corresponding-side ratios; Example 4 solves an inscribed corner square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The rotated square requires two similarity ratios and substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a sufficient network of implications to establish equivalence, introducing diagonals and selecting congruence and parallel-line converses without assuming properties still being proved.

questions.mappingNote: This question extends that taught proof structure to equivalent parallelogram tests.
questions.methodNote: The rhombus demonstration uses triangle congruence, corresponding angles and the converse of the alternate-angle result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a complete implication cycle linking four parallelogram characterisations.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the specified proof chain, selecting SSS then SAS and transferring corresponding angles before using equal supplementary angles to conclude perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed result is the perpendicular-diagonal property of a kite, established by successive SSS and SAS proofs.
questions.methodNote: Use equal sides to establish congruence, then corresponding angles; the question scaffolds the second congruence and straight-angle conclusion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: A scaffolded chain of SSS and SAS proofs establishes perpendicular kite diagonals.

classification.difficultyReason: Devise auxiliary constructions for the base-angle proofs. The equal-diagonal converse requires an unsupplied bridge from parallelism and equal diagonals to equal legs, through similarity and segment ratios or another geometric construction.

questions.mappingNote: Each part proves an isosceles-trapezium property or its converse; formal geometric proof is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use triangle congruence, corresponding angles and sides, and alternate-angle converses as demonstrated in Example 1. The matched teacher answer additionally supplies perpendicular constructions and similarity for part d.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Four geometric proofs include auxiliary constructions, converse statements and a similarity argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise equal radii and vertically opposite angles as SAS data, then choose corresponding alternate angles to prove parallelism. The question supplies both triangle pairs and the concluding route.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply the parallelogram definition through SAS proofs using equal radii and vertically opposite angles.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 1: establish triangle congruence, identify corresponding equal angles, and apply the converse alternate-angle property to prove parallel sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Two guided SAS proofs use circle radii and vertically opposite angles to establish both pairs of parallel sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Relates the circumcentre and circumradius to the geometry of a right-angled triangle.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied catalogue skill concerns triangle centres. This question assesses circumcentre and circumradius geometry without requiring vectors.
questions.methodNote: The circumcentre is equidistant from the three vertices; equal distances establish a circle through those vertices. The worked proof establishes the required equal distances geometrically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relates the circumcentre and circumradius to the geometry of a right-angled triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct perpendicular radii, recognise the square at the right-angle vertex, and transfer equal tangent lengths to express the hypotenuse as two segments involving the unknown radius.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed supplied skill is applying tangent properties to derive the inradius.
questions.methodNote: Use perpendicular radii to the sides, equal inradii and congruent right triangles. The matched teacher solution splits the hypotenuse into tangent segments of lengths a−r and b−r.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses perpendicular radii and equal tangent lengths to derive an algebraic expression for the inradius.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint supplies the area decomposition, but the altitude identity requires recognising that all three base–altitude products equal twice the same area and substituting these into the reciprocal inradius expression.

questions.mappingNote: Area-of-triangle is the closest supplied skill for both the area–inradius proof and its altitude consequence.
questions.methodNote: The incentre has equal perpendicular distances to the three sides. Join it to the vertices and add the three triangle areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires two general proofs connecting triangle area, inradius and three altitudes.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies the taught perpendicular-bisector construction to locate an unknown circle centre.

questions.mappingNote: Chord-properties is the closest supplied skill: perpendicular bisectors of chords pass through the centre.
questions.methodNote: Construct the circumcentre as the intersection of perpendicular bisectors of two triangle sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the taught perpendicular-bisector construction to locate an unknown circle centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the altitude using Pythagoras, connect area and perimeter to the inradius, and recognise that the two centres coincide so the circumradius is the remaining portion of the altitude.

questions.mappingNote: Unknown-sides-angles-figures is the closest supplied skill for deriving the two exact radii. The area identity from question 3 supplies the inradius step.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of circumcentre and incentre, perpendicular and angle bisectors, equilateral symmetry and triangle area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives exact inradius and circumradius from equilateral-triangle symmetry and area.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove both directions by connecting angle and perpendicular bisectors. The converse requires constructing perpendicular feet and combining equal vertex distances with equal side distances in RHS congruences to force all sides equal.

questions.mappingNote: Formal congruence proof is the directly assessed skill; triangle-centre terminology supplies the context.
questions.methodNote: Use perpendicular bisectors for equal vertex distances, perpendicular distances for the incentre, and RHS congruence to establish bisector and equal-side conclusions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires both directions of a proof about triangle centres using congruence and bisector properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Beyond the supplied four-piece construction, devise a mechanism for every larger piece count and justify it inductively. This requires handling the equilateral exception, including a separate five-piece construction, without a suggested route.

questions.mappingNote: Triangle decomposition and its geometric justification are primary; induction is secondary in the supplied solution.
questions.methodNote: Use equal distances from the circumcentre to the vertices to identify isosceles triangles. The matched teacher solution then proposes induction for part (b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines a circumcentre construction with a general decomposition proof.
